item.title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements
item.dc:creator: Xinrui Li, Pawan Sasanka Ammanamanchi, Siddharth Bhat, Rianna Jamdar, Yongxi Lin, Stella Biderman
item.description:
Implements a deterministic Lean 4 metaprogram and a proof-term auditor that judge equivalence of autoformalized Mathlib statements on ProofNetVerif.
Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq

item.title: Sharp Bounds on the Winner's Bias under Independent and Nonnegatively Correlated Noise
item.dc:creator: Ivan Viakhirev, Kirill Borodin, Grach Mkrtchian
item.description:
All theorems, corollaries and lemmas on sharp winner's-bias constants are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, in about 7,900 lines with no sorry.
Reporting the best of $M$ noisy, unbiased scores overstates the winner's value by up to $c\sqrt{V}$, where $V$ is the total noise variance and the sharp constant $c$ depends on how the noise is dependent. It was known only at the two extremes, arbitrary dependence ($\sqrt{(M-1)/M}$) and i.i.d. noise. We determine it for two classes in between: for independent, not identically distributed noise it is $\sqrt{(M-1)/(2M)}$, and for pairwise nonnegatively correlated noise it is $(M-1)/M$; for uncorrelated noise this answers the maximum version of an open question about the expected range. Explicit finite constructions attain both. As a corollary, the bias of the cross-validation estimator is bounded sharply within each class. All theorems are formally verified in Lean 4. Across 448 language-model and classifier selection pipelines, designs with per-candidate items realize a median 0.75 of the independent-class ceiling. At a fixed item budget, scoring all candidates on shared items is markedly less optimistic than giving each candidate its own items.

item.title: A frame-indifferent rank-one convex function in three dimensions which is not quasiconvex
item.dc:creator: Sergio Conti, Georg Dolzmann, Patrick Dondl
item.description:
The main theorems (1.1 and 2.1) were formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib. The formalization was written entirely by Claude Opus 5.5 under author guidance.
We construct a function $W:\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}\to\mathbb{R}$ which is frame-indifferent, $W(QF)=W(F)$ for all $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$, rank-one convex, but not quasiconvex. In a neighbourhood of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ the function is an explicit polynomial of degree four in the strain $F^TF-\mathrm{Id}$; the failure of quasiconvexity occurs at $F=\mathrm{Id}$ through a third-order mechanism of Šverák type, with test functions whose gradients are arbitrarily close to $\mathrm{Id}$. The polynomial is obtained from a geometrically linear example, a rank-one convex, non-quasiconvex quartic polynomial of the symmetric part of the gradient, by evaluating it at the strain $\frac12(F^TF-\mathrm{Id})$, adding a uniaxial prestress and a cubic correction, and enlarging the quartic term. The local function is extended to all of $\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ by adding a frame-indifferent polyconvex function which vanishes near $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. This work was carried out with the assistance of the AI model Claude Opus 5.5; the proofs of the main results have been formally verified in Lean 4.

item.title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
item.dc:creator: Jiyuan Tan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Jose Blanchet
item.description:
Agentic pipeline that autoformalizes research papers into Lean against Mathlib, with author decisions on ambiguities and repairs; includes a fully verified case study.
Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.

item.title: Verified Pauli-Product Measurement Compilation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation
item.dc:creator: John Zhuoyang Ye, Jens Palsberg
item.description:
Mechanizes QPPM semantics, Hoare logic, verified lowering and optimization, and approximation bounds in Lean with Mathlib, and uses Lean kernel-checked certificates on benchmarks.
Fault-tolerant quantum compilers implement gates through Pauli-product measurements and classical feedback. Verifying such a compiler requires reasoning about the quantum state and the recorded outcomes together: a correction reads an outcome, a gate's internal outcomes must be hidden from its caller, and an application's outcomes must survive optimization. We introduce QPPM, a language for Pauli-product measurement programs, with a weakest-precondition semantics over store-indexed matrix assertions, following quantum Hoare logic with classical variables. Every program terminates, so the Hoare logic is a syntactic presentation of weakest preconditions whose soundness and relative completeness are immediate. Its value is that component specifications compose. All results are mechanized in Lean. We verify lowering of Clifford+$T$ circuits to QPPM with private outcomes and supplied magic states, and an optimizer that eliminates measurements, fuses and reorders rotations, and schedules logical rounds while preserving every outcome that subsequent code can read. A compositional approximation relation bounds the effect of synthesis error on specifications and on output trace distance, and a certificate-checked pipeline selects, among synthesized circuits that meet the user's error limit, the one with the lowest certified depth bound. On QASMBench, verified fusion and scheduling reduce logical measurement depth by a median of 17.9%, and complete source-to-QPPM allowances are certified for all 35 valid selected small-suite inputs.

item.title: Finite Mass Response to Vanishing Perturbations at Cauchy Horizons
item.dc:creator: Yi-kun Li
item.description:
The paper's mathematical results and proofs on mass response at Cauchy horizons are formalized in Lean 4, with a public repository and verification instructions.
Smooth transverse perturbations with vanishing $L^p$ norm, for fixed finite $p\ge4$, can leave a finite positive mass increment at a Cauchy horizon. We prove this at a critical surface-gravity relation in the spherical Einstein–Maxwell–scalar system with positive cosmological constant. Each solution has bounded mass and local finite-energy weak extensions. The response escapes every fixed time window. An analytic law determines its delay and duration, and resolves enhancement or cancellation for overlapping packets.

item.title: On the proof of the Kozma-Nitzan conjecture
item.dc:creator: Jean-Baptiste Gouéré
item.description:
Cites a third-party Lean 4/Mathlib formalization of θ(p_c)=0 for Bernoulli bond percolation on Z^d, the result the exposition concerns.
In this short note, we give an exposition of the recent proof of the Kozma-Nitzan conjecture provided by OpenAI.

item.title: Hitting time for loose Hamilton cycles in the random hypergraph process
item.dc:creator: Jared León, Xizhi Liu
item.description:
Provides a Lean 4 formalisation, produced largely by an LLM, of the hitting-time theorem for loose Hamilton cycles in r-uniform hypergraphs with (r-1)|n.
The random hypergraph process starts with an empty hypergraph on $n$ vertices and adds a uniformly chosen missing edge at each step. For even $n$, we prove that, with high probability, a $3$-uniform loose Hamilton cycle appears when the last isolated vertex disappears. The approach developed here adapts arguments from Kahn's work on perfect matchings. It can also be extended to obtain the corresponding hitting-time theorems for $r=2$ and every fixed $r\ge4$ satisfying $(r-1)\mid n$. Furthermore, it can be used to estimate the numbers of loose Hamilton cycles at these hitting times for every fixed $r\ge2$, up to a factor of $\exp\{o(n)\}$.

item.title: AssureCode: Structured Justification for Trustworthy Agentic Coding
item.dc:creator: Logan Murphy, Wilson Sy, Rhys Balevicius, Kelsie Fung, Karenna Kung, Aren A. Babikian, Marsha Chechik
item.description:
Uses Lean as the formalization backend and theorem prover for autoformalized intent specifications, decomposition-soundness proofs, and test-oracle alignment checks in agentic coding.
The use of AI-based tools in software development is rapidly changing how software is produced, enabling large volumes of code to be generated with limited human implementation effort. However, this raises fundamental challenges for ensuring that generated artifacts are aligned with developer intent and have been appropriately validated. In this work, we propose the use of structured argumentation in driving AI-assisted software development. Inspired by techniques from assurance engineering for safety-critical systems, we define a language of justification rationales that explicitly relate informal natural language prompts, formal specifications, assumptions about developer intentions, and program analysis evidence in a structured and verifiable format. We then describe AssureCode, a tool-supported methodology for creating such rationales as part of agentic code generation. We provide an empirical analysis of our implementation where we investigate its capacity to contribute towards justified assurance of correctness for AI-generated code.

item.title: Residue Sums Modulo Products of Two Distinct Odd Primes
item.dc:creator: Haobo Ma, Mircea Merca, Wenlin Zhang
item.description:
Lean 4 formalizations, with a pinned public repository, verify a counterexample to Merca's Conjecture 1 and prove his lifted prime-modulus residue-sum Conjecture 2.
Let $S_m(a)$ denote the sum of the least positive residues in one multiplicative period of $a$ modulo $m$, of length $k$. We study the equality $S_m(a)=mk/2$ for $m=pq$, where $p,q$ are distinct odd primes and $k$ is even. Complementary pairing settles subgroups containing $-1$; the remaining cases depend on their embedding in the two local unit groups. At index four, we exclude mixed cyclic subgroups with biquadratic annihilator and classify every eligible imprimitive quartic kernel using two odd integer moments at its prime conductor. For each fixed conductor, the proportion of admissible second primes giving equality is $1/4$ or $1/2$; full coset balance has proportion $1/4$. For primitive quartic characters, classical triangular character-sum identities yield explicit short-sum criteria, and the relative class-number formula gives an obstruction to a centered coset. At index six, we give structural counts and construct an infinite family modulo $19q$ in which nonzero sextic and quadratic moments cancel. These applications use a standard odd-character expansion, which also recovers the known index-two balance classification and determines the sign of its deviation. A reproducible census for $pq\le10000$ counts $75\,090$ eligible cyclic subgroups and identifies $101$ mixed index-four subgroups whose own sum is centered although some coset sums are not.

item.title: When Do Gaussian Priors Fail? A Latent Geometry Investigation of RL Fine-Tuning
item.dc:creator: Wang Ru
item.description:
Lean 4 with Mathlib machine-checks the algebraic skeleton of the paper's theory, including the width-center formula, the crossover identity and the limit claims.
Latent diffusion models almost universally place a Gaussian prior on the VAE latent space. For base generation this default is unproblematic; under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, however, it carries a structural limitation. The standard VAE's KL term does not merely ignore mode structure - it actively taxes separation and tightness. When data are multimodal, the ELBO optimum compresses distinct modes into an overlapping latent. RL fine-tuning amplifies this overlap: the score network is under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, dynamic-to-variational amplification rises sharply, and the collapse boundary beta_c is pushed far above its variational scale. On the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution, a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at beta_c = 0.224 while a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior collapses at 0.00316, a 71x gap from the same pipeline. We trace this gap to a single geometric mediator, d_min/(2 sigma_0), and verify the causal chain through controlled interventions: moving geometry at fixed prior, and switching prior at matched geometry (full mediation; prior-label coefficient 0.995x, 95% CI [0.79, 1.25]). A three-source decomposition localises the amplification to the learned policy (zero ODE-solver contribution, bounded anchor mismatch); the coverage plateau is an unconditional benefit of mode-separating priors that no amount of RL capacity recovers. The remedy is conditional: a non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry would fall into overlap and the task is coverage-sensitive. A machine-checked theory skeleton supports the KL pricing structure - a divergent compactness tax under a Gaussian prior versus a finite assignment fee under a mixture - and the position-versus-plateau distinction delimits what is finite-resource from what requires changing the prior.

item.title: Thin-Layer Dichotomy in Three-Phase Mullins-Sekerka Flow: Gap Dynamics and Composite Interfaces
item.dc:creator: Tokuhiro Eto
item.description:
Selected results on the fixed-mode linearized Mullins–Sekerka system were formalized in Lean 4, with AI assistants helping develop the formalization.
We study the thin-layer limit of the Mullins-Sekerka flow in concentric circular geometries at fixed wave number $k$, contrasting a two-phase annulus with a genuine three-phase layer. A dichotomy emerges: for $k\ge2$ the rates blow up like the inverse thickness when the same phase lies on both sides of the layer, whereas between two different phases the matrix governing the linearized Fourier mode extends analytically to zero thickness. Both cases share the singular Dirichlet-to-Neumann factor of the thin annulus and differ only in whether the Gibbs-Thomson law forces an order-one potential difference across it. In the three-phase case the pure thickness-modulation rate stays below the logarithmic growth rate of the mean thickness, for every $k\ge1$ and all positive tensions, and, after projection onto the mean displacement and the outer interface, the collapsed pair moves as one interface carrying the sum of the two tensions. All statements concern the instantaneous fixed-mode linearization. The singularity is a property of the phase coupling, not of the thin geometry.

item.title: Can Reciprocal RIS Perform as Non-Reciprocal RIS?
item.dc:creator: Matteo Nerini, Juan Vidal Alegría, Bruno Clerckx
item.description:
All lemmas, theorems, and corollaries on reciprocal versus non-reciprocal RIS were formally verified in Lean 4 with Claude's assistance; code released on GitHub.
Yes, if and only if some optimal non-reciprocal RIS (i.e., maximizing a given performance metric) makes the round-trip channel transmitter-RIS-transmitter symmetric, which holds if the channel transmitter-RIS has rank one or if single-stream transmission is optimal.

item.title: Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
item.dc:creator: Carlo Ciliberto, Alessandro Rudi, Enrico Tassi
item.description:
Provides a Lean 4 mechanization of the PC2 framework and its compliance theorems; agents submit Lean proofs checked by the Lean kernel before tool calls run.
AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another's agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent's interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.

item.title: New Directions in Irrationality
item.dc:creator: Elyasheev Leibtag, Hila Barkan, Rotem Kalisch, Shachar Weinbaum, Michael Shalyt, Ido Kaminer
item.description:
The irrationality-measure bounds for ζ(2), ζ(3) and Aζ(3)+Bζ(4) are formally verified in Lean 4, assuming the prime number theorem, with sources released.
Since Apéry's proof of the irrationality of $ζ(3)$, decades of work have explored integrals, hypergeometric identities, and recurrences with exceptional arithmetic properties, to discover the strongest quantitative bounds on irrationality measures for zeta values and related constants. Yet, most findings have relied on specially tailored families of such constructions, making their systematic extension difficult. Here we show how these constructions can be connected and generalized into a common multidimensional structure based on conservative matrix fields (CMFs), enabling a systematic discovery of new irrationality proofs and quantitative bounds for irrationality exponents. CMFs are finite-dimensional cocycles of compatible rational matrix shifts, and are shown to capture all the classical constructions developed since Apéry as one-dimensional trajectories. The initial point encodes the mathematical constants; varying the trajectory within a suitable convergence region produces different approximation schemes for the same constants. We use this structure to improve the irrationality measures of famous constants, yielding for example $μ(ζ(2))<4.62675$ and $μ(ζ(3))<5.4197$, and proving that $1,ζ(3),ζ(4)$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$, yielding $μ(Aζ(3)+Bζ(4))<66.3$ for every $(A,B)\in\mathbb{Q}^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$. The same approach demonstrated over other CMFs provides irrationality proving trajectories for infinitely more mathematical constants. We further construct higher-rank CMFs with explicit initial states for $1,ζ(2),ζ(3),\ldots,ζ(d+1)$, and identify the arithmetic conditions needed to obtain further, higher-order independence results.

item.title: On the Accuracy of Approximate Leave-One-Out with Blockwise Nonsmooth Regularization in High-dimensions
item.dc:creator: Honghao Lin, Songbin Liu, Arian Maleki, Vahab Mirrokni, Chen Shang, David P. Woodruff, Hanbo Yang, Wenjin Zhang
item.description:
The main theorem's proof, initially produced by an automated agentic system, comes with a Lean 4 verification provided as a linked artifact.
Approximate leave-one-out (ALO) refers to methods that provide computationally efficient and statistically accurate approximations to leave-one-out risk estimation. These methods have recently attracted increased attention because of their connections to other important problems, including machine unlearning and data valuation. For empirical risk minimization, ALO methods often rely on a few Newton steps and therefore require smooth loss functions and regularizers. In high-dimensional problems, however, regularizers are frequently non-smooth. This has motivated the development of heuristic ALO methods for non-smooth regularization, whose empirical accuracy is often strong but whose theoretical justification remains limited. In this paper, we study the accuracy of a heuristic ALO method for a broad class of non-differentiable penalties that promote block sparsity in the proportional high-dimensional regime. Assuming uniformly bounded block sizes, we prove that the expected average absolute discrepancy between the exact leave-one-out loss and its ALO approximation is $O(\log^{3/2}(en)/\sqrt{n})$. Our proof technique differs substantially from existing approaches and relies on obtaining sharp bounds on the number of active groups whose status changes between the full-data and leave-one-out estimators. In addition to yielding stronger guarantees under weaker assumptions than prior work, our analysis provides new insight into the stability of sparse estimators under perturbations of the training data.

item.title: The algebraic and geometric classification of $3$-Poisson algebras
item.dc:creator: Hani Abdelwahab, Kobiljon Abdurasulov, Ivan Kaygorodov
item.description:
The multiplication tables of both classification theorems were checked formally in Lean 4, with the Aristotle AI system assisting the formal verification.
$3$-Poisson (ternary Nambu–Poisson) algebras are the algebras of observables of Nambu mechanics, the generalization of Hamiltonian mechanics in which the time evolution $\dot f=\{f,H_1,H_2\}$ is governed by two Hamiltonians and preserves the phase volume; their $3$-Lie part also gives the gauge algebra of the Bagger–Lambert–Gustavsson model of multiple M2-branes. We give the algebraic classification of complex $4$-dimensional $3$-Poisson algebras (seven algebras) and of complex $5$-dimensional nilpotent $3$-Poisson algebras ($38$ algebras and one one-parameter family) with both multiplications non-zero. We also describe the algebraic counterpart of the Inönü–Wigner contractions of physics: the variety of complex $4$-dimensional $3$-Poisson algebras has dimension $16$ and seven irreducible components, one of which is the orbit closure of the simple $3$-Lie algebra of the M2-brane model, and the variety of complex $5$-dimensional nilpotent $3$-Poisson algebras has dimension $20$ and five irreducible components.

item.title: A Type System for Communication-Safe Hardware Design
item.dc:creator: Aditya Ranjan Jha, Jason Zhijingcheng Yu, Umang Mathur, Prateek Saxena
item.description:
The Pact type system's metatheory proofs are mechanized in Lean 4, with the mechanization archived on Zenodo alongside the compiler.
Hardware components communicate through clock-cycle-sensitive protocols. Hardware Description Languages (HDLs), however, provide limited support for expressing these protocols or for checking that independently developed components agree on them. When components disagree, the composed design can perform unsynchronized exchanges or stop making progress. We call these failures communication-safety violations. Communication safety is therefore a global property, determined by interactions between multiple components. This makes it difficult to check modularly. This paper presents Pact, a typed extension of Anvil for modular verification of communication safety in synchronous hardware. Pact types describe message-passing, control-flow, and clock-cycle behaviour. Each component is checked against its type. Compatible types then guarantee that the components compose into a communication-safe system. Pact also supports incremental design. It can check a subsystem before the full system context is available. The check produces a summary type that captures the communication behaviour left for future compositions. To reduce annotation burden, Pact infers types by abstracting payload values while preserving communication, timing, control, and fairness. These inferred types are optimal for the checker: whenever some checker-accepted types can prove compatibility, the inferred types can prove it as well. Type inference and type checking are decidable, and compatibility is decided by a sound and complete algorithm. We implement Pact by extending the Anvil compiler and evaluate it along four dimensions: detecting communication errors during incremental design, expressiveness on ten clock-cycle-accurate translations of open-source hardware IPs, compatibility-checking time, and generated hardware overhead. Pact expresses realistic protocols and verifies all ten benchmarks in reasonable time.

item.title: Exact Compilation and Resource Laws for Hidden Integer Feedback
item.dc:creator: Ganxuan Yang, Siqi Wen, Shuyan Yu, Jidong Yuan
item.description:
Verifies the discrete-Gaussian mass, negative-floor arithmetic, hidden-rounding mixture and transcript semantics in Lean 4.19.0 with pinned Mathlib.
Hidden randomized rounding couples the privacy loss of successive integer releases. We study a rational-feedback mechanism under predictable signed-unit participation and full observation of every physical output. A preparation's lifetime connects three results. First, preserving complete carries until an observed echo synchronizes the worlds gives exact finite-law point compilation, with support-width exponent $3C-2$ at every fixed budget $C\ge2$. Second, releasing commitments earlier gives a monotone hierarchy whose exact endpoint, strict gaps and numerical brackets quantify calibration loss. At one fixed discrete Gaussian, a loss allowance of 0.09 requires all four commitments. Third, legal regeneration yields an unrestricted KL rate with a square-root testing remainder and a complete asymptotic frontier under joint physical-time and participation constraints. At fixed rational parameters, finite-window occupation programs approximate that frontier to error $2^{-b}$ in polynomial bit time in $b$. Verified countable-transcript semantics and independently checked finite certificates support these analyses. A matched static workload illustrates the resulting design tradeoff: a structured finite integer matrix improves error and fresh randomness, while the scalar feedback instance retains fewer noise-state and source-table bits.

item.title: Power-of-two cycles in projective cubic graphs of large edge-width
item.dc:creator: Jean-Fran{\c c}ois Culus
item.description:
An extension lemma and a sumset inclusion for twelve profiles listed in an appendix were formalized in Lean 4; the main theorem was not formally verified.
Heckman and Krakovski proved that every 3-connected cubic planar graph contains a cycle of length 2^m for some 2 $\le$ m $\le$ 7. We extend this to 3-connected cubic graphs embedded in the real projective plane with face-width at least three and edge-width at least 48; the cycle may moreover be taken contractible. The argument passes to the spherical double cover, where the planar theorem provides the cycle inside a subgraph of diameter at most 47, and the condition on the edge-width guarantees that this subgraph projects injectively.

item.title: The e-positivity of $\mathrm{rowDiv}_k(e_μ)$
item.dc:creator: Per Alexandersson, Lilan Dai
item.description:
The main e-positivity theorem and the closed-walk coefficient formula are formalized in Lean 4, with a public GitHub repository.
We prove that the partition division operator $\mathrm{rowDiv}_k$ preserves e-positivity, resolving a conjecture of Alexandersson and Dai. For $μ\vdash kn$ and $ν\vdash n$, we express the coefficient of $e_ν$ in $\mathrm{rowDiv}_k(e_μ)$ as a normalized sum of positive rational weights over closed walks on a finite directed graph of $k$-restricted partitions. The proof combines the Pieri rule and a root of unity factorization for Macdonald polynomials. As a corollary, we recover the h-positivity of the symmetric functions $A_{n,k}$ of Amdeberhan, Shareshian, and Stanley.

item.title: The minimum number of vertices of a triangulation of $\mathbb{RP}^5$
item.dc:creator: Xinrui Chang
item.description:
Several intermediate statements of the computer-assisted lower-bound proof have Lean 4 proofs; the full theorem is not formalized end-to-end.
We give a computer-assisted proof that every finite simplicial triangulation of real projective five-space has at least twenty-four vertices. Together with the construction of Guyer, Steinerberger, and Yang, this determines the minimum. A cup-product argument produces an induced subcomplex on sixteen or seventeen vertices. Transfer to the spherical double cover then imposes a covering condition on its lifted faces. In the sixteen-vertex case, a direct capacity bound excludes twenty-two vertices. For twenty-three vertices, a cochain extension argument reduces every relevant completion to one of 115 critical signed complexes; integer weights and exact covering certificates exclude all of them. The argument requires no assumption that the triangulation is combinatorial.

item.title: Non-Acceleration of the Heavy-Ball Method in 1D
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos Fotopoulos, Michael Helcig, Karl Deck, Jannis Alsbach
item.description:
The main arguments on heavy-ball cycling and 1D non-acceleration are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with the formalization generated entirely by AI.
Despite having an asymptotically optimal rate of convergence on convex quadratics, the acceleration of Polyak's heavy-ball method and a characterization of its dynamics within more general settings have remained long standing open problems. Recently, the work of Goujaud et al. [Math. Program. (2025)] made progress regarding acceleration in the context of smooth, strongly convex minimization: for a small enough inverse condition number, either the method does not accelerate on quadratics, or there exists a smooth strongly convex function such that heavy-ball cycles over the roots of unity. The constructed functions have two variables, thus leaving the question of acceleration over univariate functions open. In this work, we use a Fourier-based analysis to i) provide a proof for the non-acceleration of the heavy-ball method over the class of univariate smooth strongly convex functions. We also ii) provide a strict enlargement of the previous root-of-unity cycling region, with insights regarding the "fractional" sets of Goujaud et al. [arXiv:2502.19916], and iii) give a higher dimensional cycling instance which is not covered by root-of-unity cycling.

item.title: Structure-Aware Equivalence for Evaluating Autoformalized Statements
item.dc:creator: Yi Yu, Yu-Hsuan Wu, Guang Lin, Yuhui Zhang, Yuxiang Peng
item.description:
ACE normalizes and aligns Lean statement pairs, generates Lean proof obligations, and certifies equivalence or inequivalence only when Lean checks the proofs.
Evaluating autoformalized mathematical statements requires determining whether a candidate preserves the mathematical claim intended by a trusted reference. Existing methods approach this problem from complementary directions: reference-free learned evaluators estimate semantic agreement but are not constrained to a formal equivalence relation, while reference-based proof methods typically employ whole-statement logical equivalence to provide formal certificates, which is too coarse for translation fidelity and may identify mathematically unrelated statements. We introduce Structure-Aware Equivalence (SAE), a role-preserving formal equivalence relation between syntactic and whole-statement logical equivalence that allows formally justified reformulations while preserving translation-relevant mathematical structure. We operationalize SAE in the Autoformalization Correctness Evaluator (ACE), which provides certified equivalence or inequivalence judgments and reports Inconclusive otherwise. On ProofNetVerif, a benchmark introduced with BEq+, ACE retains substantial equivalent-case coverage while remaining highly conservative in certifying disputed or inequivalent pairs. On targeted diagnostics, BEq+ accepts 94-96% of unrelated but whole-statement logically equivalent pairs, while Mathesis LeanScorer accepts 42% of localized meaning-changing perturbations; ACE accepts none of either set as equivalent.

item.title: Efficient Quantum Algorithm for Mixed-State Quantum Geometry
item.dc:creator: Chenyang Wang, Qi Zhao, Xiao Yuan, Xiaoxia Cai
item.description:
Lean 4 is used to formally verify the bulk–edge deduction behind the asymptotic relation β_K/(4K)→1 for the Gauss–Laguerre LCU coefficient norm; code is available on request.
Mixed-state quantum geometry plays a fundamental role in quantum metrology, multiparameter estimation, and the characterization of quantum many-body systems. Yet, unlike its pure-state counterpart, accessing mixed-state geometry requires solving an ill-conditioned Lyapunov equation for the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD), posing a major challenge for resource-efficient quantum computation. Here we address the challenge and develop a novel quantum algorithmic framework for efficiently accessing the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) and quantum geometric tensor (QGT) of mixed states. Our key insight is to uncover a previously unexplored connection between the positive semidefinite structure of density matrices and exponentially convergent Gauss-Laguerre quadrature, enabling an efficient integral-based construction of the SLD. A rigorous complexity analysis further establishes the resource efficiency of our algorithm, demonstrating logarithmic precision dependence and double-logarithmic ancillary-qubit overhead at fixed conditioning. Building on this construction, we achieve near-Heisenberg precision scaling for diagonal QFI estimation without quantum phase estimation and construct unified block encodings of the full QFIM and QGT under a bounded spectral-gap assumption. A complementary regularized algorithm extends efficient diagonal estimation to exponentially small spectral gaps under a bounded-response condition. Our results establish a resource-efficient route to coherent mixed-state quantum geometry, enabling its direct integration into quantum linear-algebra algorithms without classical reconstruction and opening new possibilities for quantum-enhanced multiparameter metrology.

item.title: Random Tournaments Are Asymptotically Almost Surely Link-irregular
item.dc:creator: Lily Zhang
item.description:
Both main results, existence of link-irregular tournaments for n≥9 and the a.a.s. link-irregularity of random tournaments, are formalized in Lean 4 (GitHub).
Bastien and Khormali (2025) conjectured that a nontrivial link-irregular tournament with $n$ vertices exists if and only if $n \ge 6$. Their work establishes the conjecture for $n \le 100$. We present a probabilistic argument for the existence of link-irregular tournaments with $n$ vertices when $n \ge 9$ to resolve the conjecture. In fact, we show that a random tournament is asymptotically almost surely link-irregular.

item.title: Surface corrections and vortex energetics in the Thomas–Fermi limit of a self-bound unitary Fermi superfluid
item.dc:creator: Bao-Duy Le
item.description:
Algebraic and functional-analytic steps of the main theorem, Bogoliubov reductions, unit conversions and power counting were checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
We study a spin-balanced unitary Fermi superfluid bound by an attractive $1/r$ interaction within an extended Thomas–Fermi density functional. Its large-particle-number limit is the Lane–Emden polytrope of index $3/2$. We prove the leading gradient correction to the ground-state energy and strong convergence of the density amplitude. A rescaled surface problem predicts the next energy correction and the leading integrated density error. Matching a vortex core to the polytropic bulk gives the energetic threshold of a singly quantized central vortex, including the constant beyond the leading logarithm. Linearizing the same surface problem predicts a local energetic threshold for collective surface excitations that, in the natural TF frequency units, decreases more slowly with particle number than the central-vortex threshold. Radial stationary, spherical Bogoliubov–Poisson, and axisymmetric real-time calculations test the predicted energy corrections and vortex matching, and resolve finite-size surface-mode minima whose approach to the continuum surface coefficient is followed to $N\simeq4\times10^6$. For the reference gradient coefficient the vortex constant is $c_1=-0.535$, and the surface Landau scale is $1.417\,ω_K(\hbar_{\rm eff}^2/2R_{\rm TF})^{1/6}\propto N^{-1/9}$; sector energies at $N\simeq4.6\times10^5$, computed after the fit, agree with the extrapolated vortex threshold to $10^{-4}$. These results distinguish the accuracy of the Thomas–Fermi bulk from the gradient physics that controls the surface and vortex core, and separate vortex energetics from the open problem of nonlinear vortex entry.

item.title: A note on the rectangular Schoenberg-Whitney theorem for clamped B-splines
item.dc:creator: Shutao Tang, Zixuan Zhao
item.description:
An attempted Lean formalization of the published proof uncovered the incorrect inequality; no Lean artifact is described.
Wang et al.(Computer-Aided Design 40 (2008) 999-1008) proposed a knot-subsequence characterization of full row rank for rectangular B-spline collocation matrices. We identify an incorrect inequality in their Appendix proof, which invalidates the argument as written, and make explicit the endpoint and multiplicity conventions on which the criterion depends. The defect lies in the proof, not in the underlying result, which is valid under suitably stated hypotheses; in the lofting construction of Wang et al. these hypotheses are implicitly satisfied, so the lofted curves are unaffected. We state the corrected result and give a new proof, independent of the disputed argument, for clamped B-splines of arbitrary degree with continuous interior multiplicities. In our proof, sufficiency follows from inclusion of spline spaces and knot insertion; necessity selects independent columns and builds the reduced knot vector from them. The proof uses no recursive column-selection construction.

item.title: Pfaffian Positivity for Convex Kernels and Optimal Matching Bounds
item.dc:creator: William Johnson
item.description:
Part of the Pfaffian positivity results is formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib. The public repository maps the Lean theorems to the paper's results.
We show that for all positive, nonincreasing, convex functions $f : (0, \infty) \to (0,\infty)$ and for any collection of $n$ points $x_i \in \mathbb{R}$ with $x_1 < x_2 < \ldots < x_n$ and $n$ even, the Pfaffian of the skew matrix defined by $f(x_j - x_i)$ above the diagonal is positive. More generally, we establish coefficientwise nonnegativity for Pfaffians arising from interval decompositions, which also yields quantitative lower bounds for singly and doubly bordered Pfaffians. Choosing $f(r) = r^{-2}$ proves the three nonvanishing assertions in the conjecture of Albouy and Moeckel. Further, we show that the rainbow bound (the product over the nested matching $\{1,n\}, \{2,n-1\}, \ldots \{n/2, n/2 + 1\}$) is the unique single-matching product that bounds $\mathrm{Pf}(A_f(x))$ below uniformly over $x$ and $f$ positive, nonincreasing, convex.

item.title: Computing Multi-Slot First-Price Pacing Equilibria at Scale via Entropic Smoothing
item.dc:creator: Yuchen Xie, Shenyinying Tu, Yuan Gao, Yi Zhang, Deepak Kumar
item.description:
All lemmas, propositions, theorems and corollaries of Sections 3–5 are machine-checked in Lean 4 using Mathlib and the Optlib optimization library.
Pacing equilibria describe how budget-constrained advertisers clear an ad market, but computing one at production scale is hard when every request fills several slots: the allocation jumps whenever two campaigns' scores cross. We consider the first-price pacing equilibrium (FPPE) of auctions with $K$ homogeneous slots and unit-demand campaigns, whose Eisenberg-Gale dual reduces, via a TopK identity, to a convex program over bids. Regularizing each request's allocation with the binary (Fermi-Dirac) entropy gives a smooth, strictly convex dual whose gradient is exactly spend minus budget and whose evaluation splits into independent one-dimensional threshold solves, one per request. The smoothed equilibrium converges to the hard one at an explicit $O(\sqrt{T})$ rate, and a duality gap certifies how far any bids are from the hard equilibrium. We implement an efficient multi-GPU solver and test it on a production ad workload. We use it to compute an equilibrium price anchor: each campaign's hindsight equilibrium cost per key result.

item.title: No Perfect Randomized Composition
item.dc:creator: Alexander Meiburg
item.description:
The main total–total composition separation (a little-o statement on a subsequence of the construction) is machine-checked in Lean 4.
Does computing a composition of total Boolean functions require the product of the randomized query complexities of its factors? We give a negative answer. There are families of total functions $f,g$ such that $R(f\circ g) =Θ\!\left(\frac1{\log R(g)}\right)R(f)R(g)$ This result requires first separating linearized query complexity $\LR$, as well as noisy randomized query complexity $noisyR$, from standard randomized query complexity $R$. Both constructions essentially come from totalizing existing partial function separations, albeit via different techniques. By adapting these techniques, we also construct total functions separating every adjacent pair in the chain from sabotage $RS$, max-conflict $\barχ$, and linearised query complexity $LR$. We show that AND-of-ORs separates conflict $χ$ from max-conflict $\barχ$ complexity and makes conflict and sabotage incomparable. Finally, randomized complexity can be smaller than its composition limit $R^*$ by the maximal factor $Θ(\log R)$. The total–total composition separation is also formalized in Lean.

item.title: An algebraic proof of 1-extension
item.dc:creator: Alexander Heaton, Martin Winter
item.description:
The main results, a new algebraic proof that 1-extension preserves generic rigidity of bar-joint frameworks, are formalized in Lean 4 with an archived artifact.
We give a new proof that 1-extension preserves generic local rigidity of bar-joint frameworks in all dimensions. The proof does not use a special position argument, which makes the approach potentially useful for X-replacement in 3-space. Instead, the balancing conditions recently introduced by the first author use directed paths in the line graph, and by modifying the end of these paths, we transfer a self-stress on the 1-extended graph back to the original. Treating the new vertex as variable allows us to extract the balancing condition of the smaller graph as one coefficient of a homogeneous quadratic. A Lean 4 formalization of the main results accompanies the paper.

item.title: Degenerations of Jordan algebras
item.dc:creator: Victor Bovdi, Ivan Kaygorodov, Yury Popov, Azamat Saydaliyev, Yury Volkov
item.description:
All degenerations and non-degenerations of the classified Jordan algebras were formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib, including Nullstellensatz certificates.
We describe all degenerations of complex $4$-dimensional Jordan algebras and of complex $5$-dimensional nilpotent Jordan algebras. The proofs do not use other papers on degenerations, and all degenerations and non-degenerations were formally verified in the proof assistant Lean 4. The graph of primary degenerations of $4$-dimensional Jordan algebras has $73$ vertices and $160$ edges. The variety of $5$-dimensional nilpotent Jordan algebras is stratified into $63$ normal forms, five of which are one- or two-parameter families; together with two special members of a family this gives $65$ objects, and the graph of primary degenerations has $154$ edges. In particular, we describe all irreducible components of the corresponding varieties: the variety of $4$-dimensional Jordan algebras has $10$ irreducible components, and the variety of $5$-dimensional nilpotent Jordan algebras has dimension $22$ and $5$ irreducible components.

item.title: Irrationality Exponents of Real CM Elliptic Periods and Powers of the Lemniscate Period
item.dc:creator: Gregory V. Chudnovsky, David V. Chudnovsky
item.description:
Main CM-period determinant argument and lemniscate-power bound are verified in Lean using Mathlib, relative to explicitly stated classical uniformization, CM-lifting and theta inputs.
We give a determinant proof that every nonzero real period of a nonsingular elliptic curve over $\mathbb Q$ with complex multiplication, measured with a specified nonzero rational invariant differential, has irrationality exponent two. The proof uses an integral origin chart, matched local lengths, an actual compactification and weighted packet map, and arithmetic and analytic estimates for the same selected minor on a rectangular sublattice of the full CM period lattice. For the integral-defined lemniscate period $Ω=2\int_0^1(1-t^4)^{-1/2}\,dt$, we also give the uniform bound $μ(Ω^n)=O(n\log(2n))$ for integers $n\geq1$. Its new arithmetic ingredient clears integration denominators prime by prime while retaining the coefficient order; a one-root norm argument and an analytic estimate at algebraic centers complete the power proof. The two arguments are presented with their different charts and exact dependencies. Lean verifies the new CM determinant argument and rational normalization relative to explicit classical uniformization, CM-lifting and theta inputs; the lemniscate-power endpoint is also verified. The formalization record states the exact classical boundary and theorem references.

item.title: Formal-Informal Mathematical Alignment through and beyond Human Annotations
item.dc:creator: Noah Gießing, Ankit Satpute, Hamid Rahkooy, André Greiner-Petter, Moritz Schubotz
item.description:
Builds a dataset linking Stacks Project tags to Mathlib statements via the @[stacks] attribute, and evaluates LeanSearch retrieval plus LLM judging.
Formalized mathematics libraries such as Lean's mathlib provide machine-verifiable representations of mathematical knowledge, including definitions, theorems, and their relationships. If effectively connected to informal mathematical resources, formal mathematics could help uncover previously implicit links between mathematical concepts and improve access to existing formalizations. However, connections between informal and formal mathematics libraries are currently sparse and unsystematic. In this paper, we make first strides towards better formal integration. We construct a dataset linking informal statements from the Stacks Project to their formalizations in mathlib by exploiting expert annotations. We evaluate retrieval, LLM-based reranking, and LLM-assisted verification to discover new unannotated informal-to-formal links. To facilitate exploration and reuse of formalized knowledge, we integrated the newly discovered alignments into the MaRDI knowledge graph, enabling mathematicians to find formal counterparts to informal mathematical content. We discuss the difficulties and challenges in using LLMs for linking formal and informal mathematical content. All code and data necessary for reproducing this paper can be found at: https://github.com/AnkitSatpute/Formal-Informal-Mathematical-Alignment

item.title: The exponent $1/4$ in three complexity bounds: integer bases, continued fractions, and the $(3/2)^n$ steering word
item.dc:creator: Ralf Stephan
item.description:
All three complexity bounds and the quantitative Subspace Theorem are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, released in a public repository with a declaration-by-declaration appendix.
Let $ξ$ be a real algebraic irrational number and $p(n,ξ,b)$ the number of distinct blocks of length $n$ in its base-$b$ expansion. Bugeaud and Evertse proved in 2008 that $p(n,ξ,b)/(n(\log n)^η)$ is unbounded for every $η<1/11$. We prove this for every $η<1/4$. We also prove the analogous bound for the continued fraction expansion of an algebraic number of degree at least three, with every exponent $δ<1/4$. Bugeaud announced this statement in 2013 with an unspecified $δ>0$. Finally, the subword complexity of the steering word of $(3/2)^n$ exceeds $C\,k(\log k)^η$ infinitely often for every $η<1/4$ and every $C$. The three proofs share one count: $\varepsilon^{-1}$ classes times $\varepsilon^{-3}$ subspaces from the quantitative Subspace Theorem of Evertse and Ferretti. The subspaces are then disposed of at the cost of a logarithm, with no further power of $\varepsilon^{-1}$. All three results, and the quantitative Subspace Theorem they rest on, are machine-verified in Lean 4.

item.title: Lean Finder V2: Semantic Search for Mathlib That Disambiguates User Queries
item.dc:creator: Jialin Lu, Xiaoyu Liu, Hengrui Luo, Rodrigo Stehling, Linxi Liu, Weiran Sun, Yuepeng Wang, Wuyang Chen
item.description:
Builds a semantic search engine over Mathlib declarations, trained with adversarially generated ambiguous queries, and tests it on Lean theorem proving with Claude Code.
We introduce Lean Finder V2, a semantic search framework for Mathlib that disambiguates user queries through complementary model-level adversarial training and input-level query rewriting. Human mathematicians and coding agents rarely search Mathlib by providing detailed context. In practice, they query short properties, notation, aliases, or hypotheses, leaving much of the intended mathematics implicit. In contrast, existing Mathlib search engines unrealistically assume context-rich queries. The scarcity of real-world short queries paired with ground-truth Mathlib statements makes this ambiguity even more intractable. We argue that this is essentially a data problem. Through adversarial training, we scale up the generation of labeled short and ambiguous queries, and learn to disambiguate user queries at both model-level fine-tuning and input-level query rewriting. On the human-curated MathlibQR benchmark, our Lean Finder V2 sets a new state of the art, with at least 11% relative improvement over the previous best Mathlib semantic search engines. On top of our state-of-the-art retriever, optimized query rewriting further improves MathlibQR retrieval. On unlabeled queries from human and coding-agent interactions, Lean Finder V2 is ranked as the strongest system. Integrated with Claude Code, Lean Finder V2 improves proof success on downstream theorem-proving task. Lean Finder V2 is available at: https://leanfinder.github.io/

item.title: Global Convergence of Detailed Balanced Mass Action Systems
item.dc:creator: Haoran Lv, Chengjin Ni, Manqin Wang, Shenli He
item.description:
Formalizes in Lean 4 with Mathlib the full proof of global convergence for detailed balanced mass-action systems, about 9,300 lines, written with AI agents.
We give a self-contained proof that, for a finite detailed balanced mass-action system with positive rate constants, each positive stoichiometric compatibility class contains exactly one positive equilibrium and every positive trajectory converges to it, together with a Lean 4 formalization of the complete argument from persistence to convergence. Boundedness and persistence come from the barrier argument of OpenAI (2026) for weakly reversible systems: an arbitrary-tolerance affine approximation yields a finite-minimum barrier whose superlevel sets confine trajectories and give one logarithmic bound for all solutions from a given initial state. The Horn-Jackson dissipation identity identifies the positive equilibria as an exponential family with parameters in the orthogonal complement of the stoichiometric subspace, which gives uniqueness in each class. A bounded-speed descent argument replaces LaSalle's invariance principle; it uses neither uniqueness of solutions nor continuous dependence on initial data, and it places every cluster point in that family. The route given here is direct and elementary, and its main theorem is checked by the Lean kernel against explicit definitions. The proofs, the Lean development, and the manuscript were produced in ClawsGO Science, an agent harness that packages a complete research environment: Claude Opus 5.5 made the research decisions, GPT 6 Astra carried them out, and the Lean kernel checked every formal step.

item.title: LLM2Cert: LLM Synthesis of Certificates with SMT/Lean Verification
item.dc:creator: Zhipeng Cao, Peiyang Song, Nikolaus Vertovec, Weiru Cui, Zhihao Yang, Mingkang Liu, Luxia Lin, Bai Xue, Alessandro Abate
item.description:
An LLM Proof-Repair agent writes kernel-checked Lean proofs for Lyapunov/barrier certificate obligations that SMT solvers cannot discharge or cannot encode.
Lyapunov functions and barrier certificates give state-space guarantees of stability and safety, but synthesizing and verifying them—especially for nonlinear, high-dimensional systems—remains an open challenge. Existing pipelines verify candidates with numerical solvers (sum-of-squares programs), interval methods, or satisfiability-modulo-theories (SMT) solvers, which often require relaxations, are conservative, or scale poorly with model dimension and nonlinearity. These limitations have also shaped benchmark design: standard test suites are dominated by low-dimensional polynomial systems chosen to suit what solvers can handle rather than what engineering applications require. We address both sides of this challenge. First, we introduce DynaCertBench, a benchmark of 105 instances: 80 non-redundant systems curated from the literature, extended with high-dimensional and control-constrained variants and new nonlinearly coupled systems, comprehensively spanning stability, region-of-attraction, forward-invariance, and safety tasks. Second, we present LLM2Cert, an LLM-driven framework that synthesizes candidate certificates and verifies them against their proof obligations: each obligation is routed to an SMT solver or directly to the Lean Proof-Repair agent. On DynaCertBench, LLM2Cert verifies 81 of 105 instances ($77.1\%$), a $17.1$ percentage point improvement over one-shot proposal without feedback. On the 81 fixed certificates, LLM2Cert verifies 22 that All-SMT leaves unresolved. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/llm2cert.

item.title: Reflections on Trusting Lean
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Bresolin, Marcello Mamino
item.description:
Studies the metatheory of Lean 4's type theory and implements one direction of the arithmetic-conservativity proof in Lean 4.
It is known, by works of Werner and Carneiro, that the type theory of Lean (and indeed of CIC plus a version of choice) is equiconsistent with ZFC plus "there are infinitely many strongly inaccessible cardinals". We prove a finer connection between these two formal systems; namely, given any formula in the language of second order arithmetic, that formula is provable in the aforementioned extension of ZFC if and only if the same formula, when viewed as a type in Lean, is inhabited.

item.title: Rank Ceiling for Twiddle-Perturbation Faults on the Forward NTT
item.dc:creator: Chakshu Gupta
item.description:
A Lean 4 and Mathlib artifact certifies the one-fault-per-layer rank-and-kernel theorem for the forward NTT at n=256 with arbitrary replacement values, plus inverse-NTT kernel equalities.
NIST standardised ML-KEM and ML-DSA in 2024 for post-quantum key establishment and digital signatures. Both compute forward number-theoretic transforms (NTTs) on secret polynomials. Published attacks zero every fixed multiplier, or twiddle, during Kyber key generation with a single fault, or individual twiddles in one Dilithium signing variant; countermeasures detect or mask these faults. Nonzero replacements preserve invertibility, but the uncompressed correct-minus-faulted transform difference can still expose input information. This paper characterises the linear map from a secret polynomial to this difference under arbitrary static twiddle replacements, including bit-flips. For one fault, rank equals the number of butterflies sharing its twiddle, halving by layer from 128 to 2 for ML-KEM and to 1 for ML-DSA. Known positions, replacement values and the difference determine that many independent linear combinations of input coefficients. With one fault per layer, all but the constant and linear coefficients for ML-KEM, or the constant for ML-DSA, are determined; Lean 4 certifies this rank-and-kernel result. Those coefficients cancel for every fault set and choice of replacement values. NIST permits seed storage, motivating comparison of a known correct key with a released faulty key from the same seed. If only one ML-KEM secret-polynomial NTT is faulted, the key difference is a known matrix column times the transform difference; an invertible column entry reconstructs the latter. For ML-DSA, neither reconstruction nor the number of secret-polynomial candidates from compressed key differences is established. The per-layer ranks give a closed-form measure of raw exposure for countermeasure design.

item.title: Lean-QuantumAlg: A Framework for AI Agents to Produce Quantum Algorithms that Humans Can Trust
item.dc:creator: Lei Zhang, Mingrui Jing, Yusheng Zhao, Jiahong Liu, Xin Wang
item.description:
Builds a Lean 4 framework on Mathlib for certifying quantum algorithms' correctness and resource bounds, with nine AI-formalized algorithms.
AI agents are increasingly capable of constructing quantum algorithms and proofs, yet machine-checked proofs alone cannot guarantee that the intended problem is solved or that resource claims match the verified computation. Here we introduce Lean-QuantumAlg, a Lean 4 framework for trustworthy AI-assisted development of quantum algorithms. Its Algorithm-Solves-Problem contract binds correctness, success probability, borrowed-state restoration and quantum and classical resource bounds to a single execution, while separating the guarantees that Lean checks from the problem specifications and execution models that humans review. We demonstrate the framework on nine AI-formalized quantum algorithms, from Grover search to quantum attacks on RSA-2048 and P-256, with less than 1% of each algorithm's imported source code requiring statement-level human review once the shared framework has been audited. By integrating reusable mathematical foundations, certified algorithmic primitives and execution-grounded verification, Lean-QuantumAlg provides a basis for AI agents to construct and certify quantum algorithms, opening a path toward scalable AI-driven discovery of quantum algorithms.

item.title: Agentic Verified Optimization of Real-World Software
item.dc:creator: Zhe Ye, Udaya Ghai, Zhizhen Qin, Dawn Song, Soonho Kong
item.description:
Agents write faster Lean 4 implementations with kernel-checked equivalence proofs against reference functions, including C/C++/Go/Rust programs migrated into Lean.
Program optimization aims to improve performance while preserving behavior. Coding agents can already make programs faster by changing algorithms, data structures, and execution strategies. However, existing equivalence checks mostly rely on tests, which agents have been shown to exploit, passing the tests without preserving the intended behavior. We propose agentic verified optimization, in which an agent produces a faster implementation together with a machine-checked proof of equivalence to the existing one. Because the existing implementation serves as the specification, the task avoids the specification-writing bottleneck of verified code generation, and recent advances in theorem proving make the proofs attainable. We formulate the task at the function and repository levels in Lean 4, where programs can be both executed and reasoned about. Few real-world applications are written in Lean, so we develop Aqueduct, an agentic framework that migrates C, C++, Go, and Rust programs into native Lean, validates each port by differential testing against its original. On the 189 reference implementations in Verina, agents produce faster proved rewrites for 156, including algorithmic changes such as replacing exponential recursion with dynamic programming. On 17 migrated applications, their 92 proved rewrites speed up 47 of 51 application scenarios. These application-level gains are smaller than the function-level ones, making the choice of functions to optimize an important problem. Current agents can thus already carry out verified optimization on both standalone functions and applications migrated from real programs. We discuss the remaining challenges and the steps toward verified optimization in production.

item.title: The algebraic and geometric classification of semi-alternative superalgebras
item.dc:creator: Hani Abdelwahab, Ivan Kaygorodov, Roman Lubkov
item.description:
Lean 4 is used to check the polynomial identities showing that super Sagle cubics follow from the semi-alternative equations, a key lemma.
The algebraic and geometric classifications of complex $3$-dimensional semi-alternative superalgebras are given. As corollaries, we obtain the algebraic and geometric classifications of complex $3$-dimensional $\mathfrak{perm}$, associative, and assosymmetric superalgebras.

item.title: The End of Consensus Research?
item.dc:creator: Clément Burgelin, Rachid Guerraoui, Zicong Hong, Yinan Hu, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Rafael Pires, Rasmus Moorits Veski, Martijn de Vos
item.description:
An AI agent harness formalizes consensus protocols in Lean and proves linearizability, using about 135K lines of Lean that include proofs for a new protocol and counterexamples for existing ones.
Consensus is a fundamental problem in distributed computing and at the core of state machine replication (SMR). Despite decades of active human research, discovering practical low-latency solutions to the problem is still open, as it requires combining protocol knowledge, correctness reasoning, implementation, and experimental evaluation. We report on how AI helped us discover A-greement, a new consensus protocol for geo-replicated state machines that significantly outperforms state-of-the-art solutions. Averaged across six deployments with 5 or 9 replicas, A-greement reduces the mean latency of a geo-distributed key-value store over the fastest baseline by 12.2% and 33.3% on write-heavy and read-heavy workloads, respectively, and matches the fastest baseline on read-only workloads. A-greement combines lease-authorized local reads, direct client learning for leader-ordered writes, and a fast fixed-quorum per-key write path, selected according to network topology and workload. At the heart of our discovery lies AI-greement, an agent harness for the "autonomous" discovery, implementation, experimentation, and verification of candidate protocols. AI-greement integrates (1) a concept-oriented protocol knowledge base, (2) a modular implementation skeleton, and (3) a Lean-based verification framework with reusable safety definitions, reference specifications, and proofs. AI-greement is of independent interest: its Lean formalization uncovers several previously unreported vulnerabilities in existing consensus protocols, and it provides guidelines on how domain-specific harnesses can turn general-purpose coding agents into effective tools for (distributed) computing research. Yet we argue that human consensus experts remain essential before, during, and after the search: agents reshape the researcher's role rather than end consensus research.

item.title: Formalizing Cooperation and Competition: An AI-Assisted Mathematical Addendum to a 2018 Planning Thesis
item.dc:creator: Haitham Masaud Amar
item.description:
Game-theoretic results on Nash equilibria, cores, cost of stability and regret efficiency, plus a terminating negotiation procedure, are formalized and kernel-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
We present an AI-assisted mathematical addendum to Strategic Trip Planning: Striking a Balance Between Competition and Cooperation (Amar, 2018). We reconstruct selected relationships between strategic choice, cooperative stability, participant approval and enforcement. The thesis's Nash-to-core proposition is under-specified until outsider opportunities are stated. We verify two-person implications under fixed outsiders and explicit efficiency conditions. Under isolation, the original example has an empty TU core; its funded counterpart uses an explicit external subsidy. For a monotone resource model we characterize the exact financing gap. A finite negotiation procedure implemented in Lean is proved to terminate with participant approval, joint-cost non-worsening and local optimality against permitted approved moves. Supporting formalizations address bargaining geometry and regret-based efficiency. A resource-game counterinstance shows why monotonicity alone provides no uniform price-of-anarchy bound. Reproducible computations compare a documented heuristic reconstruction with the verified procedure on 44 source-based instances and 96 starting cases from four additional synthetic network families. Acceptance-matched heuristic and randomized pairwise-search controls contextualize the optimization results. The mathematical ingredients are established results; the contribution is a traceable reconstruction linking source statements, explicit assumptions, checked proofs, executable code and retained counterinstances. The study illustrates how AI-assisted investigation can turn engineering intuitions from legacy research into precise mathematical claims whose conditions and computational consequences can be inspected and reproduced.

item.title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
item.dc:creator: Tanqiu Jiang, Min Bai, Sadat Shahriar, Wanyu Du, Sandesh Swamy
item.description:
Two integrity theorems (Action Integrity and Reasoning Integrity as noninterference) for the single-user memory interface are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface, while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate and influences the agent's behavior only through what the gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user verification effort does not rise. On $τ^2$-bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.

item.title: Depth Separation for Neural Networks under Gaussian Measure
item.dc:creator: Cynthia Bortolotto, Francisco Ganacim, Roberto I. Oliveira
item.description:
All theorems, lemmas, propositions and corollaries are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, developed with LLM assistance and checked by an axiom audit.
We revisit the problem of depth separation for neural networks, as studied by Eldan and Shamir, Daniely, and others. Specifically, we consider the natural setting of $L^2$ approximation of radial functions under the standard Gaussian measure in $d$ dimensions. We show that there is a radial function in $L^2$ under the standard Gaussian measure that can be approximated to a fixed sufficiently small $L^2$ error by a depth-3 ReLU neural network of polynomial size in $d$ but can only be approximated by depth-2 networks with subexponentially bounded weights if their size is at least exponential in $d$. For that, we prove a general result showing that if a radial function has substantial mass in the high frequencies of its Hermite expansion, then it cannot be well approximated by a depth-2 neural network with small width and bounded weights. All theorems, lemmas, propositions, and corollaries are verified in Lean 4.

item.title: Proof of the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture
item.dc:creator: Matija Bucić, Fankang He, Hyunwoo Lee
item.description:
The proof of the Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower conjecture was machine-verified in Lean 4, with the formalization to be released in the Palomar repository.
In the 1970s, Erdős and Szemerédi conjectured that for any $n \ge k-1\ge 2$, any collection of subsets of $[n]$ not containing a $k$-sunflower has size at most $c_k^n$ for some $c_k<2$. In the $k=3$ case, this follows from the work of Croot, Lev, and Pach and Ellenberg and Gijswijt on the cap-set problem, through a reduction due to Alon, Shpilka, and Umans. We prove the conjecture for every $k \ge 3$.

item.title: Eliciting Specifications: When Does Interactive Clarification Help?
item.dc:creator: Mowafak Allaham, Aditya Vempaty, Ashish Jagmohan, Prasenjit Dey, Ravi Kokku
item.description:
LLM agents clarify task descriptions before formalizing them into Lean 4 pre/postcondition specifications, evaluated on the Verina benchmark with Lean compilation and soundness/completeness checks.
LLMs can generate Lean specifications from task descriptions, but those descriptions are often underspecified or ambiguous and may omit verifier-relevant edge cases, yielding imperfect formal specifications. We study whether an elicitation agent (EA) can improve verifier-checked Lean specifications by seeking clarification from a reference-grounded simulated developer before formalization. The agent decomposes the task, identifies unresolved decisions, asks bounded clarification questions, and uses the answers to write a refined natural-language specification that an LLM formalizer then translates into Lean. On 189 Verina Lean 4 specification-generation tasks, we compare single-shot generation with elicitation under question budgets of k=3 and k=10, allowing at most three or ten EA questions per task, across same-model and cross-model configurations. The same-model Claude Sonnet 4.6 pipeline has negative strict pass@1 estimates at both budgets, showing elicitation is not a uniform accuracy booster. In contrast, the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 and Sonnet 4.6-to-Gemini 3.8 Flash pipelines have positive strict estimates. The largest strict result reaches 65.6%, a +6.3-point change (+12 tasks), in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline. Six of eight conditions have positive compile-conditional estimates, with a maximum cross-model difference of +4.9 points among compiling outputs. Treatment estimates also differ across the basic and advanced splits; the largest advanced-task change occurs in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 configuration at k=10, from 42.0% to 50.6%. Failure analysis identifies postconditions as the largest source of degradation. These findings suggest future autoformalization systems should treat elicited natural-language specifications as intermediate artifacts and optimize jointly for semantic correctness among compiling outputs and reliable translation of clarified information into Lean.

item.title: A Complete Dichotomy for $L_\infty$ Permutation Removal
item.dc:creator: Viet Hung Le, Ruilin Shi, Fan Wei
item.description:
All theorems, lemmas and constructions are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with the Lean code produced by an AI (Claude) formalize-paper workflow; repository provided.
We study the removal problem for permutation patterns under the normalized $L_\infty$ earth mover's distance. We prove a complete dichotomy. Let \[ \mathcal E =\{(12),(21),(132),(213),(231),(312)\}. \] If $σ\in\mathcal E$, then every permutation of length $n$ that is $\varepsilon$-far from being $σ$-free contains at least $\varepsilon(n-1)$ copies of $σ$; for $0<\varepsilon\le 1/16$, this is sharp up to a constant factor for all sufficiently large $n$. If $σ\in S_k\setminus\mathcal E$, then for every sufficiently large $n$ there is a permutation of length $n$ that is $1/(8k)$-far from being $σ$-free and contains exactly one copy of $σ$. Thus the usual positive-density removal conclusion fails for every nontrivial permutation pattern, but the sparse behavior is completely characterized: the minimum number of copies is linear for exactly six patterns and is one for all others. Consequently, no canonical one-sided tester that rejects only after finding a forbidden copy can have query complexity independent of the permutation length.

item.title: Non-expansive maps between unit balls that send the sphere onto the sphere are linear isometries
item.dc:creator: Kaarel August Kurik
item.description:
The main theorem and the key rigidity lemma were formally proved in Lean, with statements and proofs hosted on the Prove2Me platform.
Let $X$, $Y$ be real Banach spaces with closed unit balls $B_X$, $B_Y$ and unit spheres $S_X$, $S_Y$. We prove that every non-expansive map $F\colon B_X\to B_Y$ with $F(S_X)\subseteq S_Y\subseteq F(B_X)$ is the restriction of a surjective linear isometry $X\to Y$. Consequently, a non-expansive bijection of $B_X$ onto itself that fails to be an isometry must map some point of $S_X$ into the open unit ball, so the plasticity of $B_X$ reduces to showing that non-expansive bijections preserve norm 1. The proof shows that $F$ is Fréchet differentiable at $0$ with a surjective linear isometry $T$ as its derivative, and then proves $T^{-1}F=\mathrm{id}$ using a quantitative rigidity lemma for non-expansive self-maps $H$ of $B_X$ satisfying $\|a+H(a)\|=2$ for $a\in S_X$; the latter relies on the Baillon-Bruck rate of asymptotic regularity for Krasnosel'skii-Mann iterations. As a corollary, the identity is extremal in the set of non-expansive self-maps of $B_X$ for every Banach space $X$, which together with a result of Bargetz, Dymond and Pirk shows that all surjective isometries of $B_X$ are extremal, answering a question of theirs, including the case of $L^1[0,1]$.

item.title: Irrationality exponents of logarithmic numbers: Values, quotients, and graded approximation
item.dc:creator: Gregory V. Chudnovsky
item.description:
Supplies a Lean supplement checking endpoints for all 62 numbered results: 53 directly checked endpoints or compositions, and nine relying on named classical theorem inputs.
We establish degree-dependent irrationality-exponent bounds for logarithms at algebraic arguments and sharper bounds when conjugate logarithms match. A two-torus construction gives an upper bound of three for ratios of logarithms of multiplicatively independent positive rational numbers. We also treat normalized quadratic logarithms and circular logarithms. The rational-logarithm and rational-power exponent-two cases were treated earlier by Liu, Jiang and Zhang; we retain them within the broader framework and its Lean verification. Starting from the interpolation and determinant method in OpenAI's September 24, 2026 preprint on the irrationality exponent of $π$, we track the arithmetic cost of algebraic embeddings and the effects of matching conjugate logarithms. A second, graded Pade construction gives near-optimal measures for powers and bounded-degree polynomial values at sufficiently small logarithmic arguments, with estimates uniform in both coefficient height and rational denominator. We state the branch, independence, parameter-order, and approximation-field hypotheses explicitly. The Lean supplement has reviewed endpoint correspondences for all 62 numbered results: 53 direct checked endpoints or compositions, and nine applications with named classical theorem inputs. Native proofs of those inputs and separate formalizations of every unnumbered assertion are not supplied. Appendix A gives the exact declarations, hypotheses, and verification evidence.
